as_told.title: Bill Gunston: Brown's work went into the B-2

plain: A respected British aviation writer named Bill Gunston is said to have written that America's B-2 stealth bomber could not fly as well as it does on its engines alone. The suggestion is that it gets a hidden boost from electrogravitics, the idea that high voltage can push against gravity. That idea is tied to Townsend Brown, an American inventor. The story comes mainly from Nick Cook, a British aviation journalist. He calls it "this astounding article." He says that when you run the B-2's weight and engine figures, "it would have been incapable of the performance figures credited for it." Cook links the article to the publications Military Power and Air International. In a later retelling he says only that Gunston found the B-2's performance data "does not add up," with no word on electrogravitics. Michels also tells it, and dates it differently. He places the article in Air International magazine in 2000, and says Gunston was "very sure" Brown's work had made it into the B-2. If true, it would mean a working gravity-defying technology was already flying in a US warplane.
